meta.source: adidas, Annual Report 2025: consolidated income statement and balance sheet (31/12/2025)
meta.disclaimer: Items grouped into the course's simplified template (the report's €1m rounding gap is allocated to other operating payables). Depreciation (D&A) = reported EBITDA − operating profit. The scenarios are educational and do not describe actual Adidas projects.
meta.cashFlowNote: 2025 published cash flow statement, regrouped into the course template: CAPEX = property, plant and equipment (363) and intangible assets (114); disposals = fixed assets (4) and disposal group (100); other investment flows = investments (−88) and interest received (58); new loans = bond (498) and short-term borrowings (166); dividends = adidas AG shareholders (357) and minorities (42). The report's rounding gaps (€1m) are allocated to the "other" lines.

taxRateNote: 2025 effective rate: €443m of tax / €1,820m of income before tax.

popUpStore.title: Adidas Originals pop-up store
popUpStore.story: Adidas opens a pop-up store for a retro sneaker collection. Fit-out €300,000 depreciated over 5 years, cost €20 per pair, selling price €100, permanent stock of €3,000, salaries €20,000/month, miscellaneous €5,000/month, minimum cash €2,000, 1,000 pairs sold per month, corporate tax at 25%. Pessimistic scenario: 100 pairs per month.

runningWorkshop.title: Adidas running-shoe assembly workshop
runningWorkshop.story: An Adidas workshop assembles 2,400 pairs over the year; the finished-goods stock rises from 140 to 270 pairs; selling price €150. Components per pair: upper 20, midsole 30, outsole 10, heel counter and lining 15, assembly 20, laces 5, insole 5, box 5 (€110). Salaries €60,000 + social security contributions €30,000. At year end, the premises are sold for €230,000 (bought €200,000 three years ago, depreciated over 40 years). A €12,000 loan at 5% is fully repaid at year end. Corporate tax at 35%.

twinSubsidiaries.title: adidas.com versus the wholesale subsidiary
twinSubsidiaries.pdfOrigin: The twin companies A and B
twinSubsidiaries.story: adidas.com collects from online customers immediately but pays its suppliers on credit: its WCR is negative and becomes a resource when activity doubles. The wholesale subsidiary holds a lot of stock and gives retailers payment terms: when its sales double, its WCR doubles too and, without financing, a bank overdraft appears. Balance sheets in €m, year Y then Y+1.

waccCase.title: Adidas simplified: WACC and value creation
waccCase.story: Simplified economic balance sheet in €bn: fixed assets 6.5 + WCR 3.5 = equity 6 + net debt 4. Adidas borrows at 6% before tax (corporate tax 33.33%), i.e. 4% after tax; shareholders require 14%. Three typical years: NOPAT of €1.0bn, €1.7bn or €0.6bn.

soleRnD.title: R&D on a new sole
soleRnD.story: Adidas invests €100m in the R&D and industrialisation of a new sole foam. Expected free cash flows: €25m a year for 5 years, zero residual value.

flagshipStore.title: New flagship store
flagshipStore.story: Opening a flagship store: €20m of fit-out, 8-year useful life, zero residual value. Additional EBITDA of €3m a year for 8 years. Straight-line depreciation over 5 years. WCR increase of €2.5m in the first year, recovered at the end of the project. Corporate tax at 40%, required return 10%.

exclusiveProjects.title: Shanghai flagship or padel line?
exclusiveProjects.story: Two mutually exclusive projects (€m). Shanghai flagship, low risk, required return 5%: −40, 10, 12, 14, 16. Padel apparel line, moderate risk, required return 7%: −30 then 10 a year for 5 years.

cashFlow2025.title: Adidas 2025: where did the cash go?
cashFlow2025.story: Adidas's real 2025 cash flow statement, regrouped into the course template (€m). The four questions of the ENGIE exercise apply… with the opposite conclusion: ENGIE had a negative result but plenty of cash; Adidas has a good result but operating cash crushed by the WCR.

acquisition.title: Buying a competitor
acquisition.story: Adidas (fictitiously) wants to buy a competitor. The price is the enterprise value paid; the target brings an EBITDA equal to the price divided by the multiple paid. Financing: debt (long-term bonds or a short-term bridge loan) or a capital increase. Benchmark from the course: Europcar 2019, very poor solvency.

dcfAdidas.title: Is Adidas worth its share price?
dcfAdidas.pdfOrigin: Exercise 1 – Group Crit (DCF, multiples, BUY / HOLD / SELL)
dcfAdidas.story: Normative 2025 FCFF = EBITDA − tax computed on EBIT − CAPEX (stable WCR). Over 5 years, the business grows at the chosen pace: EBITDA, tax, CAPEX and WCR follow, and the WCR increase consumes cash. Beyond that, perpetual growth g. Equity value = EV − net debt (€3,937m, leases included), compared with the market capitalisation at 31/12/2025.

rubberHedge.title: Adidas's rubber in 6 months
rubberHedge.pdfOrigin: Derivatives: futures and forwards (copper example) and options (Heineken call)
rubberHedge.story: Adidas must buy 10,000 tonnes of natural rubber in 6 months for its soles. Spot price today: €1,500/t. It fears a rise. Two possible hedges: buy a futures contract at €1,550/t, or buy a call with a €1,550/t strike for an €80/t premium. Educational figures.

strideLab.title: Stride Lab raises funds
strideLab.pdfOrigin: Control of the power when the startup raises equity
strideLab.story: Adidas created Stride Lab a year ago with €10m of share capital: 10,000 shares with a €1,000 nominal value, all held by Adidas. The prototype works: €90m are needed to industrialise, raised from venture capital funds. Fictitious start-up and figures, transposed from the course example (×1,000).

liquidation.title: What if Stride Lab went bankrupt?
liquidation.story: Three years later, Stride Lab is in cessation of payments; the court orders its liquidation. The assets are auctioned. Claims (€m): State 3, post-filing creditors 5, bank secured on the plant 25, suppliers and other unsecured creditors 30; shareholders contributed €100m. Fictitious figures.

guessCompany.title: Recognising a company from its balance sheet
guessCompany.pdfOrigin: Exercise: Guess which company it is (p. 74-76)

hints.A: 86% tangible assets (high-voltage lines) financed 50% by debt: regulated, predictable cash flows and solid collateral.
hints.B: 47% trade payables: mass retail collects from customers in cash and pays its suppliers on credit (negative WCR).
hints.C: 33% inventories (wines and spirits ageing for years) and 33% intangibles (the brands).
hints.D: No inventory, 58% receivables (the loans granted), 65% customer deposits and 8% equity: a bank.
hints.E: 29% inventories (sneakers in transit and in warehouses) and right-of-use assets of leased stores in tangible assets: a brand distributor, between manufacturer and retailer.
